summary: This document describes threats to location information, especially for emergency calls, and techniques that improve its reliability and security. It also offers guidelines for judging how trustworthy a location is.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7378 looks at how the location a device reports can be trusted, and how it can be faked. It lists the ways an attacker lies about position, reviews three ways of protecting location, and explains how an emergency call centre can judge how much to believe what it receives. It is a set of findings and recommendations rather than a protocol.

questions: how can attackers fake emergency location
subtitle: How location claims in emergency calls can be faked, and how to tell how much to believe them.

tldr.problem: A mobile phone can put a location of its own choosing into an emergency call, and the emergency call centre has no way to tell a genuine position from a fabricated one.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7378 names the ways location is faked, reviews three ways of protecting it, signed location, location sent as a reference, and location added by a proxy, and then explains how a call taker can judge how much trust to place in what arrives.
tldr.outcome: The document is guidance rather than a protocol. It notes that no mechanism is universally applicable, that location-by-reference is the most developed, and that call centres remain exposed to denial of service whatever the location says.

facts.label: Location steps in an emergency call

today: RFC 7378 is an Informational RFC published in December 2014, and the unit metadata lists no document that obsoletes or updates it. It is a survey of threats and of existing mechanisms rather than a specification, so it can be read as a description of the state of the discussion at that time.

sections.title: Why Location Needs to Be Trustworthy
sections.content:
Several public and commercial services need location to work, among them fire, ambulance and police services, food delivery and roadside assistance. For a landline, and for a Voice over IP service that only places emergency calls from a stationary device, the location given to the Public Safety Answering Point is found by looking up the calling telephone number. For those cases, forging the caller identification can make the call centre send help to the wrong place, and that problem is being studied by the Secure Telephone Identity working group. Another existing check is for the call centre to call the caller back.

With IP-based emergency services from phones that move, the location may instead travel inside the call itself. The document's aim is that a call taker should be able to judge, in real time, how much trust to place on the information in front of them, which covers the automated location that arrives with the call, the location the caller states, and the identity of the caller or device. Where that real-time judgement is not possible, it should still be possible afterwards to work out where the call came from, so that people can be held accountable.

For this, the document defines its terms. A trustworthy location is location information that can be attributed to a trusted source, has been protected against modification while in transit, and has been assessed as trustworthy. The device whose position is tracked is the Device, the person or thing being tracked is the Target, and the network entity that works out where a device is and tells it is the Location Information Server, or LIS. The source of the information is the LIS, the node or the device the recipient obtains it from.
sections.plainLanguage: The document defines the word it is about: a location is trustworthy if it came from a source you trust, if nobody could alter it while it travelled, and if someone has checked it. It also fixes the vocabulary, so that a device is the phone, the target is the person in it, and the location server is the part of the network that works out where the phone is.

sections.title: How Location Can Be Faked
sections.content:
Three adversary models are distinguished. In the external model the end host is honest and the attacker sits somewhere between the host and the location server, or between the host and the call centre, while none of the emergency service infrastructure acts maliciously. In the malicious infrastructure model, elements such as the location server, the infrastructure that maps locations to call centre addresses, or the call routing elements act maliciously. In the malicious end host model, the end host itself acts maliciously, whether its owner knows or not.

Because attacks on infrastructure and on snooping in transit have already been described elsewhere, this document concentrates on the malicious end host. It does not cover hosts that get their location from civilian GPS, which can be spoofed, or from third-party location providers that may be attacked or may not be accurate enough for emergencies. Nor does it cover inadequate infrastructure, such as a stale wiremap or an out-of-date access point database, or a provider that looks up location using the wrong identity.

Three forms of location spoofing are named. With place shifting, the attacker claims to be somewhere else entirely, sometimes within the coverage of a particular cell tower. With time shifting, the attacker reuses a location that was true in the past but is not true now. With location theft, the attacker captures someone else's location, possibly including its signature, and presents it as their own, which can be a single incident or continuous, as when the attacker controls the victim's device, and can be combined with time shifting.

Identity matters because the threat of punishment discourages hoax calls; calls from pay phones get more scrutiny. Two kinds of identity matter for calls on an IP network: the network access identity, which might be established when the device connects, and the caller identity, which might be established at the application layer by the phone itself. If the caller did not authenticate itself to the voice provider, accountability may rest on the network access identity, and that may not have been authenticated either, as with an open wireless access point. Even when an IP address or MAC address was logged, tying it back to the owner may be hard. Because emergency calls are time-critical, multi-layer authentication is undesirable, so in most cases only the device that placed the call can be identified, and adding credentials for emergency use costs money and administration and is only useful if everyone deploys them.
sections.plainLanguage: The document sorts attackers into three kinds depending on where they sit, then focuses on the one that matters most: the phone itself lying. A phone can claim to be somewhere else, claim to be somewhere it used to be, or replay a location it stole from someone else. Whether anyone can be held responsible also depends on how the phone identified itself when it joined the network.

sections.title: Three Ways to Protect Location
sections.content:
The first technique is signed location-by-value. The location server signs the location object before sending it to the target, the target conveys it, and the recipient verifies the signature. A proposal to add a validity element, with the time the information was validated and the time the signature stops being valid, would limit replay. The cost of that is that even a stationary target must fetch a fresh object periodically, or accept the delay of a query during an emergency call. The document notes that the only proposal in this area is an expired straw-man, so the mechanism is not suitable for deployment at the time of writing. Signing also cannot stop an attack that uses valid location: a compromised host could flood a call centre with emergency calls, each carrying correctly signed location, and the work of verifying every signature could overwhelm it. It is also hard where the host uses GPS, since a host can pretend to have GPS.

The second technique is location-by-reference. The host holds a reference to the location rather than the location itself, and the recipient, typically the call centre, fetches the location from the server over a confidential and integrity-protected channel. This avoids modification by the host or an intermediary, saves the host from querying the server repeatedly, and lets an operator charge for the location instead of handing it over. The reference carries a random component so that third parties cannot guess it, and references must expire so that a recipient cannot track a host permanently and so that the server can reclaim them. TLS must be used for dereferencing unless some other mechanism provides confidentiality and integrity, and the recipient must authenticate the host identity using the domain name in the location URI. Two authorisation models exist. Under authorisation by possession, knowing the URI is enough, and the server can allow any request that presents it; the secret must therefore be protected in transit, and once granted, access cannot easily be revoked. Where hiding the location matters, authorisation by access control lists is preferred, which needs the call centre to hold credentials for every location server in its area, so a certificate hierarchy rooted in the valid emergency services authority, or an aggregation point that holds the relationships, would be needed.

The third technique is proxy-added location, where a proxy that can work out the end point's location, from its IP or MAC address for instance, retrieves and adds or overrides the location. This needs application-layer entities deployed by internet access providers, and a standardised profile on every device and every access provider. A proxy that adds a location takes on full responsibility for it, so it must answer any complaint about the location itself, and the new location must be placed last in the location header field. Overriding a location the host supplied is awkward, because there is no way to tell which of the two is more accurate: the host may have a GPS receiver while the proxy knows only the nearest cell tower. The access provider also has to take responsibility for emergency calls from customers it has no relationship with, which usually requires an interaction between the access provider and the voice provider that may not exist, in which case the fallback is to complete the call with no caller identity at all.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three ways to protect a location. The server could sign it, but the only draft of that has expired. The device could carry a reference instead of an address, and the call centre could fetch the real location itself over an encrypted channel. Or a proxy in the network could look up the location and add it, ignoring whatever the device said. Each has a cost: signing needs a trust hierarchy, references need expiry and secret-keeping, and proxies need to be deployed by every access provider.

sections.title: Assessing How Trustworthy a Location Is
sections.content:
Trust assessment matters even when the location is signed or fetched directly over a protected channel, because neither says whether the data is valid or where it came from. If automated location is known to be suspect or missing, the call taker can spend more effort checking the call and asking the caller. For location theft, the entity element of the location object is of little value if it holds an unlinked pseudonym, but if the location server authenticated the target, the link between the pseudonym and the target can be recovered later in an investigation.

The source of the data is the most practical signal. Location from a server whose operator has a history of meeting emergency accuracy requirements may be treated as more reliable than location from a third-party provider that disclaims emergency use. Even a provider that does not meet the emergency accuracy bar can still say something useful, for example whether the position came from the nearest cell tower or access point or from triangulation, whether the tower's position came from its owner, and when that position was last checked.

Real-time validation is also possible. The city, state, country or continent tied to the IP address in the signalling or the media source address can be compared against the location the caller reported, although only entities close to the caller may be able to check properly. The timestamp inside the location object can be compared against the timestamp of the enclosing signalling message to see whether the location is fresh, but the timestamp is only an assertion by the server, which may or may not be synchronised, and the object may have been held for a while before it was sent. Refreshing location objects to renew the timestamp puts extra load on the server, so recipients have to judge the timestamp themselves.

Accountability rests on audit logs. Where logs exist and a law enforcement agency can compel them, the owner of an unlinked pseudonym can be identified during an investigation. Where attacks are frequent and continuous, automated mechanisms are needed, such as exchanging audit trail information between providers and call centres, or heuristics that separate likely fraud from real emergencies. Applying a test to prove the caller is human is controversial, because of the risk of delaying or rejecting a genuine call.
sections.plainLanguage: Even a properly fetched location says nothing about whether it is right. The call taker has to judge it from clues: where the address in the signalling seems to be, where the location came from, whether the timestamp is fresh, and whether the provider of that location is known to be accurate for emergencies. Where the call is a hoax, the provider's logs are what allow someone to be held responsible afterwards.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Although it matters that location cannot be faked, the techniques in the document do not apply everywhere. Many devices with a GPS receiver will struggle to use any of them, and users are unlikely to want to upload their location to a nearby server for verification.

Callers can be authenticated in the signalling itself, and changes to the identity and location in transit can be detected using cryptographic mechanisms, but interoperability with Session Border Controllers that modify protected headers has been a problem, so a revision of that work was in progress. Without an end-to-end solution, SIP over TLS can give message authentication and integrity hop by hop. The value of caller authentication is limited where identities can be crafted easily, as with many VoIP offerings today, and an attacker who can forge emergency calls at low risk of accountability may be encouraged to make them.

Call centres remain open to distributed denial of service even with these techniques in place. A large number of calls that appear to come from different places is much easier to imagine with IP-based emergency services than with the legacy system, and an attacker in one country can now attack the emergency infrastructure of another. The attacks in the document can also be automated: code running on a device can read its location and place a call, or request a location object and reuse it, removing the need to be physically near the location being spoofed. To reduce that risk, providers can limit the ability of untrusted code, such as a WebRTC application written in JavaScript, to place emergency calls.

Three finite resources are exposed: the network and server infrastructure, the call takers and dispatchers, and the first responders. Even a large city may have only a handful of call takers on duty, so a call centre can be overwhelmed by a small-scale attack even if every location is checked carefully, and first responder resources are scarce, particularly during mass casualty events.
sections.plainLanguage: None of the three techniques can be used everywhere, and none of them stops a flood of calls. An attacker with control of a phone can make it call with a plausible location, and a city with a handful of call takers on duty can be overwhelmed by a small number of such calls. The document also notes that where identities are easy to fake, identifying hoax callers afterwards is much harder.

sections.title: Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
The emergency calling architecture uses the Presence Information Data Format location object, and the location privacy architecture attaches privacy rules to every location object so that whoever receives it knows how it may be used, whether that is a simple rule such as do not share my location, or a detailed preference about who may know it and when.

In practice, emergency calls cut across these rules. Because of hoax calls, anonymous emergency calls are restricted, and caller identification may be used during an emergency call, so location in a signalling message can end up linked to an identity. There are privacy concerns in the signed case too, because linking a location object to identifiers is what stops replay attacks. Observing location during an emergency call is itself a privacy risk, so the framework requires transport layer security for the signalling and for the talk with the location server, though the privacy rules attached to the location may still not apply.

In many jurisdictions a person asking for emergency help is assumed to be giving permission for the call centre and the first responders to obtain their location, so the privacy rules are waived implicitly when an emergency call starts. Likewise, any signalling entity that receives a message containing location through normal routing is treated as an authorised recipient, which means one entity may pass the location on to another. Where location is sent by reference rather than by value, stricter authorisation is possible, limiting access to intermediaries and snoopers, but that is not possible when access is granted simply by possessing the reference.
sections.plainLanguage: Location normally carries rules about who may use it and who may pass it on. An emergency call overrides much of that: asking for help is treated as permission to share the location, and any server that handles the call is treated as entitled to see it. Sending a reference rather than the location itself allows tighter rules, except when access is granted just by holding the reference.

viz.caption: THE THREE TECHNIQUES FOR PROTECTING LOCATION

cells: The location server signs the location object and the recipient verifies it
The only proposal had expired, so it was not deployable
The recipient fetches the location from the server itself
Needs references to expire, secrets protected and a way to authorise the recipient
A proxy in the network looks up the location and adds or overrides it
Needs application-layer entities at every access provider and device

viz.caption: THE THREE WAYS A DEVICE CAN LIE ABOUT ITS LOCATION

items.title: Place shifting
items.text: The device claims a position it is not at, sometimes within the range of one cell tower.

items.title: Time shifting
items.text: The device reuses a position that was true earlier but is not true now.

items.title: Location theft
items.text: The device presents someone else's location as its own, possibly with its signature.
